title: The Shampoo Sachet Is Lighter. The LPG Cylinder Costs ₹29 More. Iran's War Is Reshaping India's Kitchen Shelf.
excerpt: From Dabur shrinking packs to Maruti hiking car prices, India's consumer economy is absorbing the full force of $96 oil — and the diaspora is feeling it in remittances and airfares
body:
The shampoo sachet is lighter. The cooking oil bottle is 50 millilitres shorter. The biscuit pack has two fewer pieces. And the LPG cylinder now costs ₹29 more.

Across India, the Iran war is arriving not as a headline but as a quiet rearrangement of the kitchen shelf. Consumer goods companies are raising prices, trimming pack sizes, and cancelling promotional offers as oil at $96 a barrel sends input costs spiralling through the supply chain.

"We are among the world's most vulnerable countries," economist Jayati Ghosh warned, noting that higher oil and fertiliser costs, weaker Gulf demand, softer remittances, and potential capital outflows could all stoke inflation and slow growth simultaneously.

The Invisible Tax on Every Household

India's biggest fast-moving consumer goods companies have moved in near-lockstep. Hindustan Unilever, Godrej Consumer Products, and Dabur have rolled out low- to mid-single-digit price hikes across categories. Britannia is preparing similar moves.

But the real story is not the price tags — it is the packaging. In a country where millions of consumers buy daily essentials in ₹10 and ₹20 sachets, companies are shrinking product sizes rather than breaching those psychologically critical price points.

"We are reducing grammage because we can't breach those price points," said Mohit Malhotra, global CEO at Dabur. "A ₹10 pack of shampoo needs to stay at ₹10. The only variable is what's inside."

This pattern — known globally as shrinkflation — hits India's lowest-income consumers hardest, because they are the ones buying single-use packs.

From Oil Fields to Kitchen Shelves

The chain is direct. Brent crude has risen 3.5 percent to $96.5 a barrel after Iran launched missiles at Israel, closing off hopes of a ceasefire and raising fears of Strait of Hormuz disruptions. India imports roughly 85 percent of its crude oil.

The rupee, already under pressure from capital outflows, has weakened further — amplifying the cost of every dollar-denominated import from petrochemicals to palm oil.

The government raised domestic LPG prices by ₹29 per cylinder on Saturday, bringing the Delhi retail price to ₹942. The Oil Ministry disclosed that actual supply costs have risen to over ₹1,600 per cylinder, creating an under-recovery of approximately ₹700 on every unit sold. Global LPG prices have jumped 46 percent since February, driven almost entirely by Hormuz route disruptions.

This is the second LPG hike in three months. The opposition Congress party called the government a "recovery government" that was making households pay for a war they did not start.

Automakers and Airlines Feel the Squeeze Too

The pressure extends well beyond grocery aisles. Maruti Suzuki, Mahindra & Mahindra, Tata Motors, and Hyundai Motor India have all hiked vehicle prices.

"We were left with no choice," said Partho Banerjee, Maruti's senior executive officer for marketing and sales. "Raising prices is not good for customers, especially first-time buyers."

Airlines IndiGo and Air India are trimming capacity on fuel-heavy international routes and increasing fares to offset aviation fuel costs. For the diaspora, this means rising ticket prices on the India-US and India-Gulf corridors at the start of summer travel season.

What NRIs Are Watching

The immediate concern for Indian Americans sending money home is the weakening rupee, which now buys less against the dollar than it did three months ago. Remittances from the Gulf — India's single largest source — are also under pressure as the Gulf economies absorb the same oil price volatility.

For families in India, the arithmetic is straightforward. Cooking gas costs more. Groceries cost more or deliver less. The car or scooter EMI may rise if the Reserve Bank of India responds to imported inflation with a rate hold instead of a cut. And flight tickets home are climbing.

The government has responded with one structural measure: the Department of Consumer Affairs has prescribed nine standard edible oil pack sizes, from 200 ml to 20 litres, under the Legal Metrology framework. The goal is to make it harder for companies to quietly shrink packaging without consumers noticing. Manufacturers have three months to comply.

Whether that is enough to offset what Ghosh called "one of the most dangerous macro environments India has faced in a decade" remains the open question.

Sources: Reuters, The Hindu BusinessLine, The Hear (India News Archive), PTI
